title: An Astrologer's Day
author: R. K. Narayan
summary: Every day at midday a 'professional' astrologer spreads out his cowrie shells, a cloth with mystic charts, a notebook and palmyra writing under a tamarind tree in the Town Hall Park. Sacred ash, vermilion, dark whiskers and a saffron turban make his searching eyes look prophetic. He works by the light of the groundnut vendor's flare among sellers of medicine, stolen hardware and cheap cloth.

He knows nothing of the stars. He left his village suddenly, without any plan, and lives on 'study, practice and shrewd guesswork'. He charges three pies a question, lets the client talk for ten minutes, and gives answers about the common troubles of mankind — marriage, money and the tangles of human ties.

One night, as he is packing up, a stranger challenges him. They agree on a wager: eight annas if the answers satisfy, double if they are wrong. By the match-light the astrologer has seen the man's face and is frightened; he tries to give back the anna and leave, but the stranger holds his wrist. The astrologer then tells him that he was stabbed, pushed into a well and left for dead, and even calls him by name — Guru Nayak. He says the attacker died four months ago, crushed under a lorry, and advises Guru Nayak to go home, two days' journey north, and never travel south again.

Guru Nayak gives him a handful of coins — twelve and a half annas, not the promised rupee — and leaves. At home the astrologer tells his wife that a great load has gone from his mind: years ago, as a drunken young gambler, he had stabbed a man in his village and fled believing he had killed him. That man was Guru Nayak, who is alive.

Genre: a suspense story with a surprise ending, first published in 1947; the first story of Malgudi Days. R. K. Narayan received the Sahitya Akademi Award (1960), the Padma Bhushan and the Padma Vibhushan.
Irony: the astrologer calls Guru Nayak a 'swine' who cheated him of a rupee, though he himself has deceived Guru Nayak about who he is and about the 'dead' attacker.
Themes: superstition and gullibility, deception, guilt and redemption, the contrast of light (knowledge) and darkness (secrecy).

Present perfect continuous (has/have been + -ing) for an action continuing up to now; past perfect continuous (had been + -ing) for an action continuing up to a point in the past. Phrasal verbs (put by, put out, look after, look into …).

sa2: Describe the astrologer's appearance and how it attracted customers.

His forehead shone with sacred ash and vermilion, dark whiskers streamed down his cheeks and he wore a saffron turban. These made his searching eyes look prophetic, and people were drawn to him like bees to flowers.
How did the astrologer manage to satisfy his clients?

He let each client talk for ten minutes, which gave him material for many answers. He then spoke of common troubles — marriage, money, human ties — and flattered them, so nine out of ten agreed with him.
How did the astrologer know so much about Guru Nayak's past?
He was the man who had stabbed Guru Nayak in a drunken quarrel and pushed him into a well. So he knew about the knife, the well and even the name, though Guru Nayak thought it was astrology.
Why did the astrologer advise Guru Nayak to go home and never travel south again?
He wanted to keep Guru Nayak far away from the town where he lived, so that Guru Nayak would stop searching for his attacker and the astrologer's secret would stay safe.
What is the significance of the title 'An Astrologer's Day'?
The story follows one day in the astrologer's life, from setting up at noon to going home at midnight. That single day brings the meeting with Guru Nayak, which frees him from years of guilt.
What made the astrologer's wife happy, and what worried her?

She was overjoyed with the twelve and a half annas, as she could buy jaggery and coconut to make sweets for their child. But she noticed her husband looked worried and was shocked to learn he had once tried to kill a man.
sa3: Why did the astrologer shiver when confronted by the stranger?

When the stranger lit his cheroot, the astrologer saw his face by the match-light and recognised Guru Nayak, the man he had stabbed and pushed into a well years ago. He feared he would be recognised and punished, so he shivered in his grip and his voice grew faint.
Why is the ending of 'An Astrologer's Day' a surprise? How does Narayan prepare for it?

We learn only at the end that the astrologer himself had stabbed Guru Nayak, which explains his fear, his knowledge and his advice. Narayan prepares for it with hints: the astrologer left his village suddenly, he feels uneasy when he sees the stranger's face, and he tries to return the anna and leave.
Bring out the irony in the story.

The astrologer knows nothing of the stars yet is trusted as a prophet. He calls Guru Nayak a 'swine' who cheated him of a rupee, though he has deceived Guru Nayak completely. And the 'prediction' that freed Guru Nayak was really a confession that freed the astrologer.

or: Write a character sketch of the astrologer.

He is shrewd and observant, reading people's worries from their talk and faces. He is a fake but hard-working, earning an honest man's wage by his wits. He carries guilt for a crime of his youth, and he is quick-witted under pressure, turning danger into safety and relief.

sa3: How is the contrast of light and darkness used in the story?

The park has no municipal lights; the half-light hides the astrologer's ignorance and his identity. A match-light reveals Guru Nayak's face to him, a moment of recognition. At the end the green shaft of light vanishes, leaving darkness, as his secret stays hidden — yet he himself is relieved.
